channel.title: Acme: Light News
channel.description: Positive, lighthearted and unusual current news.

item.title: Three scientists win medicine Nobel for controlling cells with light
item.description: Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel won the Nobel Prize in medicine for optogenetics, a method that uses light-sensitive proteins as switches inside cells. The technique lets researchers turn specific neurons on and off with light, opening new ways to study the brain.

item.title: Houston Zoo welcomes a tiny parade of rare reptiles
item.description: Houston Zoo is celebrating several pint-sized conservation milestones, including its first-ever Hosmer’s spiny-tailed skink birth. New arrivals also include star tortoises, eyelash vipers and leaf-tailed geckos—an appropriately scaly cast for October.

item.title: Mars, a crescent moon and a star cluster share the morning sky
item.description: Early risers can see Mars close to a slim crescent moon before dawn on Oct. 5. The red planet is also heading toward the Beehive Cluster, a sparkling group of stars also known as M44, making binoculars especially rewarding over the next several mornings.

item.title: Manila church fills with wagging tails for annual pet blessing
item.description: Dogs, cats and other companions crowded Manila’s Malate Church for a cheerful annual blessing tied to the feast of St. Francis of Assisi. Priests sprinkled holy water over pets and their people as parishes marked the patron saint of animals with one of the calendar’s most photogenic traditions.

item.title: Steve Reich reflects on making music at 90
item.description: Composer Steve Reich, now 90, talks about his latest work and a creative life that helped redefine modern music. The interview finds him still composing, still revising his methods and still thinking carefully about what technology can—and cannot—contribute to human expression.

item.title: Zoo’s first porcupette gets the name Bramble
item.description: Visitors voted to name Point Defiance Zoo’s first porcupette “Bramble,” a nod to her prickly quills and curious nature. Born Aug. 17 to first-time parents Quillow and Nigel, the tree-climbing youngster is thriving and marks the first porcupine birth in the Tacoma zoo’s 121-year history.

item.title: Museum turns mushroom electricity into music
item.description: A new exhibition in Exeter translates electrical signals from woodland fungi into a soundscape. “Living Labyrinths” also includes Beatrix Potter’s overlooked mycology studies, a sculpture honoring a fungus named for her and an artist’s watercolor map of the fungal ecosystem inside her own body.

item.title: Comedy wildlife finalists catch animals at their funniest
item.description: The 2026 Nikon Comedy Wildlife Awards drew a record 10,000-plus entries from 112 countries. Finalists include a sneezing moose that appears to finish with a grin, a flower-wearing bird, meerkats posing for a family portrait and a young elephant receiving an ill-aimed dust bath. Winners will be announced Dec. 8.

item.title: Tiny feathered dinosaur offers new clues about flight
item.description: A remarkably complete 22-inch fossil from northeastern China has been identified as Norellraptor barsboldi, a new birdlike dinosaur species more than 100 million years old. Portions of its plumage remain preserved, including signs of asymmetrical flight feathers that may help show how flight-related traits evolved along more than one path.

item.title: Harvest Moon rises beside an erupting Mount Etna
item.description: A striking composite made near Nicosia, Sicily, captures the Harvest Moon rising at sunset while Mount Etna sends ash and gas into the sky. The scene also includes the Belt of Venus, the pinkish band caused by sunlight scattering through Earth’s atmosphere above the planet’s shadow.

item.title: Satellite finds a farming island amid vast wetlands
item.description: Landsat images show a tidy patchwork of fields around The Pas, Manitoba, surrounded by the sprawling Saskatchewan River Delta. The northern farming enclave turns from green to brown across the 2026 growing season, making human geometry stand out vividly against one of North America’s largest inland freshwater deltas.

item.title: Scientists identify a new wild cat species in Bolivia
item.description: Researchers have identified the Bolivian tiger cat, Leopardus tilcayo, as a distinct species—the first newly recognized living cat species in more than a century. Evidence so far consists of two observed animals and a handful of camera-trap records, adding an elusive new branch to the feline family tree.

item.title: NASA invites the public to hunt for overlapping galaxies
item.description: NASA's new Overlap Zoo turns a cosmic coincidence into a citizen-science project. Volunteers can inspect telescope images, verify pairs of galaxies that line up from Earth, and trace their outlines. The resulting catalog will help astronomers map otherwise elusive dust and improve distance estimates.

item.title: Space agencies begin planning a garden for the Moon
item.description: NASA and partners in Canada and Germany will design an Earth-based test bed for growing crops under Moon-like conditions. A future lunar garden could give crews fresh food while absorbing carbon dioxide, producing oxygen and recycling water—putting a practical spin on the old dream of farming beyond Earth.

item.title: Scientists map possible refuges for endangered tropical frogs
item.description: Smithsonian researchers identified places in Panama where vulnerable frogs may be able to persist despite a deadly fungal disease. The work points toward climate refuges that could guide reintroduction efforts, offering a hopeful, more targeted strategy for restoring amphibian populations.
